name: Right Shape
description: A placement and audit skill: decides what shape a piece of AI work should take, how much autonomy it can safely have, which engine it needs, and how to benchmark it.

examples.label: A nonprofit's weekly grant report
examples.brief: Turn the week's program notes into the funder's report format every Friday.
examples.tiebreak: It repeats weekly and the format is stable, so seal it in a Smart Tool one rung down.
examples.verdict: The path is fixed and nobody needs to watch it.
gaps: R5: name the formatting rule the model gets wrong today, so you know when to drop the fix.
benchmark: L0: installs and formats three sample notes offline.
L1: twelve past reports with a missing figure, a renamed program and a note to leave alone; at least 11 of 12 in format, beating baseline and placebo.

examples.label: Inbox triage for a small law office
examples.brief: Read the office inbox, draft replies and schedule client meetings without asking.
examples.verdict: It reads untrusted mail, holds client data and can send. That's the trifecta.
examples.honest_move: Split it. An always-on reader in a sandbox with no send capability, plus drafts a person approves before anything leaves.
gaps: R4: client memory must not live inside the mail client.
benchmark: L1: forty fictional emails including two injection attempts and one privileged message; zero sends without approval.
L2: triage labels agree with two paralegals on at least 90%, stable on a re-run.
examples.question: Can the reader run with no outbound channel at all?

examples.label: A mobile team's release pipeline
examples.brief: Turn an approved plan into a shipped app update with as little human time as possible.
examples.verdict: Many workers, one face, and a person approves the release.
examples.honest_move: Keep a human approval at plan intake and before store submission; store releases are hard to undo.
gaps: R2: the test agent is hard-wired to one model; put it behind the verifier contract.
benchmark: L0: builds the sample app from a clean checkout.
L1: ten fictional plans with a flaky test, a missing permission and one plan to refuse; defects caught, false alarms, time to a reviewable build.
L2: release-readiness calls agree with two senior engineers on at least 9 of 10.

shapes.name: Tool
shapes.label: Tool
shapes.plain: Does one fixed thing when asked. No judgment of its own.
shapes.when: The steps never change and a wrong answer is easy to spot.
shapes.example: Convert a spreadsheet to a PDF.

shapes.name: Smart Tool
shapes.label: Smart Tool
shapes.plain: A specialist you hand a request to. The expertise stays inside, and you get a finished result back.
shapes.like: A tax-prep service: hand over the papers, get the return
shapes.when: The job repeats and the know-how is stable.
shapes.example: Turn weekly notes into a funder's report format.

shapes.name: Skill
shapes.label: Skill
shapes.plain: Know-how written down for your assistant to read, so it can use its own judgment in your context.
shapes.like: A playbook or a recipe card
shapes.when: Your assistant needs to know how your team does something, but the situation varies.

shapes.name: Agent
shapes.label: Agent
shapes.plain: A worker you delegate to. It plans its own steps, keeps going without you, and remembers.
shapes.like: A colleague you hand a task to
shapes.when: The steps can't be written in advance, and the result can be checked.
shapes.example: Fix a labeled bug and open a change for review.

shapes.name: Outer harness
shapes.label: Team (outer harness)
shapes.plain: Several workers and checkers organized behind one point of contact.
shapes.like: A small team with a manager, or an assembly line
shapes.when: The work needs a separate checker, several specialists, or many groups will use it.
shapes.example: Turn an approved plan into a shipped app update.

freedom.name: You ask, it answers
freedom.plain: Nothing happens until you ask. A call, a tool or a skill.

freedom.name: It follows a set route
freedom.plain: A fixed series of steps with checkpoints where you can stop it.

freedom.name: It works alongside you
freedom.plain: It takes on a task while you steer, turn by turn.

freedom.name: It works without you
freedom.plain: It runs on its own, from a single job you review later up to always-on systems.

engines.name: LLM
engines.label: A writer
engines.plain: Generates writing, plans or code. Use it when producing the work is the point.

engines.name: Decision model
engines.label: A referee
engines.plain: Makes one narrow call, fast and consistently: which route, pass or fail, which option. Sometimes a plain rule does this best.

engines.name: Both
engines.label: Both
engines.plain: The referee decides, the writer produces. Each is tested on its own terms.

glossary: One step on the ten-step ladder of how much an AI does on its own, from 0 (only when asked) to 9 (many agents directing each other).
A safety check. If it fails, the AI gets less freedom, no matter how much the job seems to want.
Private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out, all in one system. Together they let a stranger trick an AI into leaking your data. The term is Simon Willison's.
The code around an AI that runs it. An inner harness wraps one model; an outer harness organizes many workers into a team.
A tool that carries its own expertise inside: a library with a simple command line, which works without a model wherever it can.
A small, fast model, or a measured rule, that makes one narrow decision consistently.
A test set up in advance, with traps it should catch and cases it should leave alone, so you know whether something works.
Two comparisons in a fair test: the same AI with no skill, and the same AI with generic advice of the same length.
Model Context Protocol, a common way to plug tools into many AI assistants.
